A Conditional Threshold Hypothesis for Creative Achievement: On the Interaction Between Intelligence and Openness
Alexandra M. Harris, Rachel L. Williamson, and Nathan T. Carter University of Georgia

Theoretical perspectives on creativity have suggested that intelligence is necessary but not sufficient for creative behavior. Known as the threshold hypothesis, this idea has generated both controversy and confusion since Guilford (1967) suggested that creativity and intelligence would be correlated more strongly among those low in intelligence relative to those high in intelligence. In this article, we instead argue for a conditional threshold hypothesis such that the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement is moderated by other critical characteristics. Further, we propose that the relationship is in fact stronger among individuals who possess high levels of qualifying characteristics. We then argue that openness to experience represents one such critical characteristic. For those with high openness, we propose that high levels of intelligence will be the differentiating factor between those who exhibit high and extremely high creative achievement. Additionally, we argue that for domain specificity, it is necessary to differentiate between the openness aspects of aesthetic openness and intellect for explaining creative achievement in the arts and sciences, respectively. Participants living in the United States (N -1,276; Mage - 34.56 years; 67% female, 82% White; 91% at least some college; 88% employed) completed the Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ) as well as fluid intelligence and personality measures. Results of Poisson analyses regressing CAQ scores onto personality and intelligence measures scored with item response theory lend full support to these hypotheses. Implications of our conditional threshold hypothesis are discussed.
Keywords: creative achievement, intelligence, openness, threshold hypothesis

Among theories regarding the relationship between intelligence and creativity, the threshold hypothesis is one of the most commonly endorsed (Kim, Cramond, & VanTassel-Baska, 2010). This hypothesis holds that intelligence is positively related to creativity until a certain level— or threshold— of intelligence, after which differences in intelligence are unrelated to creativity. However, after over a half century of research on the threshold hypothesis, it has garnered relatively mixed empirical support (Karwowski & Gralewski, 2013; Kim, 2005). Consequently, recent research on the topic has focused on correcting for methodological limitations of earlier studies to clarify findings. Such methodological short-

Another key distinction in interpreting findings regarding the threshold hypothesis concerns the distinction between creative potential and creative achievement. Creative potential is typically considered a trait reflecting one's ability to generate original ideas or products. In contrast, creative achievement concerns actualization of an individual's creative potential and is typically assessed through biographical questionnaires or other objective criteria (Eysenck, 1995). Recent research that has reviewed how methodological approaches may influence findings has shown tentative support for the threshold hypothesis as it concerns the relationship between intelligence and creative potential but not creative achievement (Jauk et al., 2013; Karwowski et al., 2016; Karwowski & Gralewski, 2013). Rather, Jauk et al. (2013) and Karwowski et al. (2016) suggested that the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement is likely to be constant across the range of intelligence. Moreover, although Mackinnon (1962) reported evidence of the threshold hypothesis for creative achievement, other studies that utilized creative achievement as the criterion did not support the traditional threshold hypothesis (Park, Lubinski, & Benbow, 2007, 2008; Robertson et al., 2010; Wai, Lubinski, & Benbow, 2005). Overall, most investigations of the

threshold hypothesis have utilized creative potential, not creative achievement, as the criterion (Jauk et al., 2013). Thus, findings regarding the threshold hypothesis and creative achievement are tentatively unsupportive but also notably limited.

Despite relatively few investigations of the threshold hypothesis involving creative achievement, researchers have long expressed interest in threshold hypothesis as it applies to creative achievement, not just creative potential. Mackinnon (1962), one of the seminal scholars on the threshold hypothesis, stated that "true creativeness" requires not just original thought but also application in the real world and execution of the idea. Mackinnon asserted, "The acceptance of such a conception of creativity... meant that we would not seek to study creativity while it was still potential but only after it had been realized and had found expression in clearly identifiable creative products" (p. 485). Likewise, in his work on creativity, Eysenck (1995) was particularly concerned with creative achievement manifest as "genius" or eminent populations exhibiting extraordinary creative accomplishments. Guilford (1967), who proposed a threshold hypothesis for the relationship between intelligence and divergent thinking, also extrapolated his observations to creative achievement or distinction "in some areas of creative endeavor, such as inventing and composing, perhaps painting" (p. 170). Clearly, the limited number of studies conducted on the threshold hypothesis for creative achievement is not reflective of overall interest in the topic.

Given the interest in the threshold hypothesis as it applies to creative achievement but unsupportive—albeit limited—findings, the current study argues for a theoretical revision of the threshold hypothesis as it relates to creative achievement. The current article establishes the theoretical foundation for a conditional threshold hypothesis that incorporates one of most central personality traits to creative behavior: openness to experience. Specifically, we propose that the traditional threshold hypothesis as it concerns creative achievement only holds true for individuals with low to moderate standings on the personality trait of openness to experience. For those with high openness, we propose that intelligence positively and more strongly predicts creative achievement above an intelligence threshold than it does below that threshold. That is, the threshold hypothesis should be inverted for individuals with high openness such that the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement strengthens rather than weakens beyond the intelligence threshold. Further, drawing on past work on creative achievement (Kaufman et al., 2016), we argue that for domain specificity, it is necessary to differentiate between the openness trait aspects of aesthetic openness for explaining creative achievement in the arts and intellect for explaining achievement in the sciences.

As commonly conceived, the threshold hypothesis suggests that intelligence is necessary but not sufficient for creativity (Guilford, 1967). Most researchers have so far interpreted this assertion to mean that above a certain intelligence threshold, intelligence no longer predicts creativity. We argue that a more faithful interpretation of the threshold hypothesis suggests that, after some intelligence threshold, other individual differences are critical for understanding the relation between intelligence and creative achievement. In particular, we argue that the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement strengthens among those who also possess high levels of

other qualifying characteristics. Thus, we propose that there are differential intelligence–creativity relationships conditioned on other individual differences. We refer to this differential influence as the conditional threshold hypothesis.

To the authors' knowledge, no other researchers have explicitly proposed a conditional threshold hypothesis for the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement, yet the hypothesis is theoretically and empirically consistent with the literature that considers both the independent and multiplicative effects of individual differences on creative achievement (e.g., Eysenck, 1995; Jauk, Benedek, & Neubauer, 2014; King, Walker, & Broyles, 1996). Researchers have long believed that creativity is a function of a complex constellation of traits and abilities (Albert & Runco, 2010). Eysenck (1995) directly suggested that a combination of not only intelligence but also environmental factors and personality traits "are needed to produce a truly creative achievement, and many of these variables are likely to act in a multiplicative (synergistic) rather than an additive manner" (p. 38). Indeed, Eysenck postulated that personality variables may explain why some highly intelligent individuals see major accomplishments and others accomplish relatively little. Even authors who are considered seminal to the foundation of the threshold hypothesis have cautioned an overemphasis on intelligence alone. For example, Mackinnon (1962) stated that "if a person has the minimum of intelligence required for mastery of a field of knowledge, whether he performs creatively or banally in that field will be crucially determined by nonintellective factors" (p. 493). Although Mackinnon's research supports a negligible relationship between intelligence and creative achievement consistent with the traditional threshold hypothesis, he also emphasized the importance of personality for creative achievement at high levels (Mackinnon, 1965). It is possible that had Mackinnon accounted for a multiplicative relationship between intelligence and these nonintellective factors, intelligence may have shown a relationship with creative achievement.1

1 Notably, one reviewer suggested that prior research indicates that not all individuals with high levels of creative achievement exhibit high levels of intelligence (e.g., Eysenck, 1995; Mackinnon, 1962) and, further, that those who earned low grades in school (which correlate with intelligence) achieved more revolutionary innovation than those who earned higher grades (Simonton, 1994). However, we contend that although individuals with high intelligence may fail to exhibit high creative achievement because they lack other critical personality characteristics (Eysenck, 1995), prior findings do not suggest such personality characteristics can wholly compensate for intelligence below a minimum threshold. As Mackinnon (1962) noted, "No feeble-minded subjects have shown up in any of our creative groups" (p. 488). Likewise, in a summary of earlier work (Cox, 1926, cf. Eysenck, 1995), Eysenck asserts that findings show "beyond any doubt that geniuses in many different lines of endeavor have uniformly IQs well above the average" (p. 59). Moreover, by using a rigorous analytical approach, Karwowski et al. (2016) have shown evidence that a minimum of intelligence is necessary but not sufficient for high creative achievement. Karwowski et al. (2016) noted that almost no participants showed high creative achievement but low intelligence. Regarding individuals who exhibit low academic performance but ultimately high creative achievement, Simonton (1994) was careful to distinguish traditional measures of academic performance (e.g., grades) from true scholastic attainment (e.g., self-directed education or research). Simonton suggested that many high achieving individuals who were poor students pursued nontraditional education, which we believe still points to high intelligence. Thus, we do not believe that evidence of some individuals' simultaneous high creative achievement and poor academic performance supports a negligible intelligence– creativity relationship.

Empirical evidence further supports the multiplicative influence of individual differences on creative achievement. Jauk et al. (2014) found that intelligence interacted with everyday creative behaviors to predict creative achievement such that only individuals who were both highly intelligent and engaged in many creative behaviors exhibited high creative achievement. King et al. (1996) similarly found support for the interactive effect of creative abilities and openness on creative achievements. Thus, both theoretical and empirical support persists for interactive effects of intelligence and other characteristics on creative achievement.

Although Eysenck (1995) suggested that creative achievement, relative to creative potential, is particularly likely to occur because of interactive effects, empirical evidence does not preclude the possibility of interactive effects on creative potential. In what has come to be recognized as the foundational work for the threshold hypothesis, Guilford (1967) presented a graph illustrating the wide range of divergent productivity scores for those high in intelligence but a narrow range for those low in intelligence. Researchers typically cite this distribution of creativity scores as supporting a negligible relationship at high intelligence levels (Karwowski & Gralewski, 2013); however, this interpretation is tentatively incomplete. Another interpretation is that there is high variability in the intelligence– creativity relationship at higher levels of intelligence. This variability in the correlation at high levels of intelligence can be interpreted as an underspecified relationship, wherein one or more moderating variables has been ignored. As shown in Figure 1, the graph first presented by Guilford is consistent with a conditional intelligence– creativity relationship. In such a moderated relationship, intelligence shows a stronger relationship with divergent productivity (i.e., creativity) as the level of a secondary characteristic increases.

Likewise, in a meta-analysis of the relationship between intelligence and creative potential, Kim (2005) suggested that results do not support a strong intelligence– creativity relationship but that moderated relationships are likely. Among possible moderators, Kim found support for the moderating influence of some sample characteristics on the intelligence– creativity relationship; for example, age moderated the relationship such that it was stronger for older samples. Although the current study concerns creative

achievement specifically, the possible support for interactive effects of intelligence and other characteristics on creative potential further highlights the complex relationship between intelligence and creativity broadly and the need to consider a more nuanced threshold hypothesis.

Although several studies show no support for the traditional threshold hypothesis applied to creative achievement, there is some support for an inverted intelligence– creativity relationship (Park et al., 2007, 2008; Robertson et al., 2010; Wai et al., 2005) such that the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement may be stronger above the threshold than below it. For instance, Park et al. (2007); Robertson et al. (2010), and Wai et al. (2005) utilized a sample of the top 1% of intellectually talented adolescents as determined by SAT scores before Age 13. Even within this sample of highly gifted youth, intelligence predicted creative accomplishments. Still, Mackinnon (1962) found support for the traditional threshold hypothesis and creative achievement, and both Jauk et al. (2013) and Karwowski et al. (2016) found support only for a relatively constant relationship between intelligence and creative achievement at all intelligence levels.

Intriguingly, some investigations of the threshold hypothesis and creative potential have also found support for an inverted threshold. Sligh et al. (2005) specifically screened for intelligence to increase the distribution of high IQ students and found that the intelligence– creativity relationship strengthened among individuals with high IQ. A possible commonality between the sample used by Sligh et al. and those used by Park et al. (2007, 2008), Wai et al. (2005), and Robertson et al. (2010) is that such samples involved selection bias, in that they were similarly characterized by high levels of traits beyond intelligence alone. If so, these results would be consistent with a conditional threshold such that among individuals who possess both high intelligence and appropriate levels of other qualifying characteristics, intelligence will show an even stronger positive relationship with creativity. On the other hand, the sample used by Mackinnon (1962) may have

Similarly, had Jauk et al. (2013) and Karwowski et al. (2016) accounted for an interaction between intelligence and openness, they may have found a strengthened relationship between intelligence and creative achievement among those high in openness and a weakened relationship among those low in intelligence. Without controlling for such an interaction, this relationship could appear constant and positive.

Despite relatively little empirical evidence that supports the traditional hypothesis for creative achievement, evidence tentatively persists for the possibility of an inverted threshold in which the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement strengthens above an intelligence threshold for those with other critical characteristics. Although research supports the role of many individual characteristics and circumstances in predicting creativity and creative achievement, we propose that openness to experience reflects one characteristic that is likely to exemplify the conditional threshold hypothesis. Next, we review research supporting openness to experience as one such qualifying characteristic. We then outline explicit hypotheses for testing the threshold hypothesis for intelligence and creative achievement conditioned on openness.

Perhaps one of the most obvious candidates for a qualifying characteristic of the intelligence– creativity relationship is the personality trait of openness to experience. Of the five-factor model (FFM) traits, only openness has consistently been shown to relate to creativity (Feist, 1998; King et al., 1996; McCrae, 1987). Further, openness has been shown to be important for creative achievement above and beyond intelligence (Feist & Barron, 2003) and to interact with other individual differences in predicting creative achievement (Jauk et al., 2014; King et al., 1996). Notably, although openness shows the strongest correlation with intelligence compared with other FFM traits (DeYoung, 2011), openness and intelligence are distinct in that individuals may score high in one while scoring low in the other (McCrae & John, 1992). Given the importance of openness for creative achievement, the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement may be dependent on openness such that individuals high in openness show a stronger relationship between intelligence and creative achievement.

Indeed, research has already shown support for a relationship between intelligence and creativity conditioned on openness. Specifically, Jauk et al. (2013) found that below an IQ threshold of 104, openness did not significantly predict creative potential. However, above that threshold, openness was the strongest predictor of creative potential (relative to other FFM traits and intelligence). Jauk et al. suggested that this finding highlights a likely interaction between intelligence and openness, "High creative potential is not possible with a low IQ; but once the intelligence threshold is met, openness may explain to some extent whether the required cognitive disposition is actually turned into high creative potential" (p. 219). Although specific to creative potential and not creative achievement, these findings support the interactive effects of openness and intelligence on creativity overall.

Drawing on our conception of a conditional threshold hypothesis and empirical evidence for an interaction between intelligence and openness in explaining creative achievement, the current study tests such an interaction. Karwowski and Gralewski (2013) identified two ways to test the threshold hypothesis: comparing intelligence– creativity correlations below and above some threshold and using regression analysis to evaluate the significance of both the linear and curvilinear terms (i.e., quadratic terms in which the linear term is multiplied by itself). The current study utilizes the latter approach, specifically moderated multiple regression in which the quadratic intelligence term is moderated by openness. That is, we expect that differential curvilinear relationships between intelligence and creative achievement will exist at varying levels of openness. Whereas the traditional threshold hypothesis predicts a curvilinear intelligence– creativity relationship that plateaus after the intelligence threshold, we expect that for those high in openness, there will be a curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement such that the relationship strengthens as intelligence increases (i.e., exhibits a nonlinear "swoop upward"). On the other hand, we expect that the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement for those with low to average levels of openness will be generally linear across all levels of intelligence. Thus, our hypothesis can be formally stated as follows:

Hypothesis 1 (H1): Openness will moderate the curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement such that for individuals high in openness, the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement will strengthen as intelligence increases.

Although openness to experience is the FFM trait that most strongly relates to creative achievement generally, creative achievements are inherently domain specific (e.g., arts vs. sciences). In considering domain specificity of creative achievement, an important distinction in the general trait of openness are its two aspects proposed by DeYoung, Quilty, and Peterson (2007). Within openness, these aspects are aesthetic openness—representing engagement with art, beauty, feelings and values—and intellect—representing engagement with intellectual pursuits involving semantic and abstract reasoning. Indeed, Kaufman et al. (2016) showed that aesthetic openness exhibits a stronger positive relationship with creative achievement in the arts, whereas intellect exhibits a stronger positive relationship with creative achievement in the sciences. Therefore, if our conditional threshold hypothesis is correct, we should expect domain specificity such that there is a moderating influence of aesthetic openness on the curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement in the arts. In contrast, the curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement in the sciences should be moderated by the aspect intellect.

Hypothesis 2a (H2a): In the arts, the aesthetic openness aspect will moderate the curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement such that for individuals high in aesthetic openness, the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement will strengthen as intelligence increases.
Hypothesis 2b (H2b): In the sciences, the intellect aspect will moderate the curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement such that for those high in aesthetic
openness, the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement will strengthen as intelligence increases.

Data were collected through Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), an online marketplace for work. Using MTurk, researchers can pay participants a small amount to complete questionnaires. Prior research has suggested that MTurk is a rapid, inexpensive, and relatively reliable way to collect data from a diverse population (Buhrmester, Kwang, & Gosling, 2011). Participants in the current study completed an online questionnaire posted to MTurk. To qualify for the study, participants were required to be living in the United States, at least 18 years old, and able to read English. Qualifications were determined using self-report. The final sample included 1,276 respondents (M_{\text{age}} = 34.56 \text{ years}, 67\% female, 82% White, 54% married/with partner). Additionally, 53% had received a 4-year college degree or above, another 38% has completed some college or a 2-year college degree, and 88% were currently employed. Of those employed, 23% reported that they held a management position.

Below we describe the measures and scoring approaches for creative achievement, intelligence, and personality. Although not relevant for behavioral count data (as in the measure of creative achievement), item response theory (IRT) scoring was used for the measures of intelligence and personality. This choice is not arbitrary, as recent evidence suggests that for multiple regression tests of moderation (Morse, Johanson, & Griffeth, 2012) and curvilinearity (i.e., quadratic terms; Carter, Dalal, Guan, LoPilato, & Withrow, 2017), IRT scoring is crucial to controlling Type I error rates and preserving power of tests.

Creative achievement. Creative achievement was assessed using the Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ; Carson, Peterson, & Higgins, 2005). The CAQ is a popular measure backed by strong psychometric evidence (Silvia, Wigert, Reiter-Palmon, & Kaufman, 2012) that assesses achievement in 10 creative domains: Visual Arts, Music, Dance, Architectural Design, Creative Writing, Humor, Inventions, Scientific Discovery, Theater/Film, and Culinary Arts. Each domain includes seven levels of achievements. Points were awarded per the seven achievement levels (i.e., 1 point for the first level and 7 points for the seventh level). The original CAQ scoring recommends also multiplying certain levels by their frequencies (Carson et al., 2005). However, in a personal communication, S. H. Carson recommended against this approach (cf., Kaufman et al., 2016), and it was not used in the present study (see Appendix for details). Scores were totaled to create an overall Creative Achievement score as well as a score specific to the arts and a score specific to the sciences. Domains assigned to the arts and sciences were consistent with Kaufman et al. (2016): Arts included Visual Arts, Music, Dance, Creative Writing, Humor, and Theater/Film, whereas Science included Inventions and Scientific Discovery.
Intelligence. Fluid intelligence was assessed using a 17-item subsample of Sandia Matrices (Matzen et al., 2010). The Sandia

Matrices are nonverbal object relations (i.e., involving one, two, or three transformations) and logic (i.e., conjunction and disjunction) problems similar to those used in the popular Raven's Progressive Matrices (Raven, Raven, & Court, 1998). Each problem asks the respondent to select the item that completes a pattern. An initial review of the relationship between the Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices and the Sandia Matrices in an undergraduate sample showed a correlation between participant scores on each measure of .69 and .83 after attenuation correction (Matzen et al., 2010). Items were selected for inclusion in the current study to reflect a range of difficulties and item types. Answers were dichotomously scored as either correct or incorrect. Overall, average proportion of correct responses for each item type was higher in the current sample than in the Sandia Matrices norming study. Matzen et al. (2010) reported proportion correct averages for each item type as .86 for 1-relation, .61 for 2-relation, .47 for 3-relation, and .38 for logic. In the current study, proportion correct averages for each item type were .95 for 1-relation, .84 for 2-relation, .47 for 3-relation, and .43 for logic.

Fluid intelligence theta values were obtained using the IRT three-parameter logistic (3PL) model. In addition to item location (i.e., difficulty) and discrimination (i.e., measurement sensitivity) parameters, the 3PL also includes a parameter that adjusts for guessing (Embretson & Reise, 2000). Thus, the 3PL is appropriate for multiple-choice assessments dichotomously scored as correct or incorrect (Waller, 1989).

Model-data fit was assessed by evaluating \chi^2/df ratios (Chernyshenko, Stark, Chan, Drasgow, & Williams, 2001; Drasgow, Levine, Tsien, Williams, & Mead, 1995) and marginal reliability statistics (Raju, Price, Oshima, & Nering, 2007). \chi^2/df ratios indicate the misfit between scores predicted by the IRT model (expected scores) and the actual data (observed scores). This statistic is evaluated for single items as well as sets of two items ("doubles") and three items ("triples") in which probabilities also account for the likelihood of endorsing specific response options for all items in the set. Evaluating \chi^2/df for doubles and triples ensures that the dependence or relationship between items is attributable to the measured trait and not to irrelevant factors (e.g., similarities in the wording of items). Acceptable fit is indicated by \chi^2/df ratios of less than 3 (Chernyshenko et al., 2001; Drasgow et al., 1995). The intelligence scale showed a mean \chi^2/df ratio of less than 3 for singles (see Table 1). Mean \chi^2/df ratios for doubles and triples were also below or close to 3 (see Table 1). Finally, marginal reliability was evaluated to determine the degree of measurement error and can be interpreted similarly to classical reliability coefficients (e.g., coefficient alpha) as the ratio of variance from the assessed trait to measurement error in the IRT-derived scores. Intelligence scores showed a marginal reliability of .72 (see Table 1).

Personality. Personality was assessed using an ideal-point measure of openness to experience developed by the authors and scored using the Generalized Graded Unfolding Model (GGUM2004; Roberts, Donoghue, & Laughlin, 2000). Ideal-point models assume that individuals are most likely to endorse items reflecting their actual standing on the trait. In contrast, dominance models assume that individuals are more likely to endorse positively worded items when they are high in the trait and negatively worded items when they are low in the trait. Items were written to reflect the entire trait continuum (i.e., low, moderate, and high levels of the trait) of each openness facet per the 6-2-1 hierarchical structure (DeYoung et al., 2007; Judge, Rodell, Klinger, Simon, & Crawford, 2013). A total of 30 items per facet were administered to participants for a total of 180 items. Scales for aspects aesthetic openness and intellect, as well as overall trait openness were then constructed by evaluating the item psychometric properties in GGUM2004. Like intelligence, modeldata fit for personality scores was evaluated using \chi^2/df ratios and marginal reliability. All scales showed adequate fit and reliability (see Table 1). Example items for the aesthetic openness aspect include "I do not enjoy dance performances" (low trait level), "Art museums are okay, but they're not my favorite pastime" (moderate trait level), and "I have a vivid imagination" (high trait level). Example items for the intellect aspect include "I prefer not to engage intellectual debates" (low trait level), "I like listening to new ideas if they are plausible" (moderate trait level), and "I love philosophical conversations" (high trait level).

CAQ scoring results in a count variable with a positively skewed score distribution (Kaufman et al., 2016; Silvia et al., 2012). Thus, the data violate the homoscedasticity assumption of linear regression. In keeping with prior studies utilizing the CAQ (Kaufman et al., 2016), the current study uses Poisson regression analysis. Additionally, to ensure the robustness of our findings, in analyzing creative achievement in the arts and sciences, we considered both the full sample and a reduced sample. In the reduced sample, we removed individuals with scores below the median to

ensure that the highly skewed data did not result in spurious effects. Consistent with the hypothesis and investigations of the threshold hypothesis using regression analysis (see Karwowski & Gralewski, 2013), moderated multiple regression analyses were used to test the significance of interactions between quadratic intelligence and linear personality terms. All appropriate lower order terms (i.e., linear terms, quadratic terms, and interactions between linear terms) were also included in analyses as controls (Cohen, Cohen, West, & Aiken, 2003). Personality and intelligence theta values were standardized prior to creating higher-order terms. Finally, consistent with Kaufman et al. (2016), we controlled for age and gender in all analyses.

Table 2 shows descriptive and skew statistics for CAQ scores, including the Total, Arts, and Sciences scores, as well as unstandardized fluid intelligence theta values. Correlations between all predictor and criteria variables are shown in Table 3. Creative achievement overall, in the arts, and in the sciences was significantly correlated with fluid intelligence (r = .14, p < .001; r = .09, p = .003; and r = .17, p < .001, respectively). Further, creative achievement in the arts was more strongly related to aesthetic openness (r = .37, p < .001) than intellect (r = .30, p < .001). Creative achievement in the sciences was more strongly related to intellect (r = .11, p < .001) than aesthetic openness (r = .07, p = .230). Additionally, fluid intelligence showed a stronger correlation with the intellect aspect (r = .08, p = .004) than the aesthetic openness aspect (r = .03, p = .348).

That is, results suggest that the form of the curvilinear relationship between intelligence and all types of creative achievement differs by level of openness. Figure 2 illustrates the relationships between fluid intelligence and creative achievement in (a) the arts and (b) the sciences moderated by trait-level openness. Consistent with H1, results for creative achievement in the arts show a curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement that strengthens as intelligence increases for those high in trait-level openness. For those average in openness, there is a more moderate, linear relationship. For those low in openness, there is little to no relationship. Also consistent with H1, results for creative achievement in the sciences show a curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement that strengthens as intelligence increases for those high in trait-level openness. For those average and low in openness, there is a positive relationship between intelligence and creative achievement until an inflection point, after which there is little relationship or a slight negative relationship between intelligence and creative achievement.

ligence and creative achievement in the arts that strengthens as intelligence increases for individuals high in aesthetic openness. Reduced-sample results show a similar, though slightly weaker, relationship between intelligence and creative achievement in the arts for those with high aesthetic openness. In both the full and reduced samples, individuals with average openness show relatively consistent, weak positive relationships between intelligence and creative achievement across the range of intelligence, and individuals with low openness show little to no relationship between intelligence and creative achievement.

Consistent with H2b, both full- and reduced-sample results show a curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative achievement in the sciences that generally strengthens as intelligence increases for individuals high in intellect. In the full sample, individuals with low and average intellect show a positive relationship between intelligence and creative achievement in the

sciences until an inflection point, after which the relationship plateaus or becomes slightly negative. In the reduced sample, individuals with low and average intellect show stronger positive relationships before this inflection point and stronger negative relationships after the inflection point between intelligence and creative achievements in the sciences.

Results of the current study fully support our hypotheses regarding a conditional threshold hypothesis. The relationship between intelligence and creative achievement was strongest among those high in trait-level openness, and the relationship exhibited a curvilinear "swoop upward." On the other hand, individuals low in openness may show a slight positive relationship between intelligence and creative achievement but are unlikely to demonstrate

high creative achievement regardless of their intelligence. Put another way, results suggest that openness matters most for creative achievement at high rather than low levels of intelligence (i.e., beyond an intelligence threshold). Moreover, for creative achievement in the sciences especially, increased intelligence among those with low or average openness is not beneficial beyond an intelligence threshold. Thus, results support a conditional threshold hypothesis in which, at high levels of intelligence, the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement is dependent on other essential characteristics. In contrast, at low levels of intelligence, these other characteristics have relatively little impact on creative achievement. Further, in contrast to the traditional threshold hypothesis, individuals show an enhanced rather than negligible relationship between intelligence and creative achievement at high levels of these qualifying characteristics. That is, results also support an inverted relationship from that proposed by the traditional threshold hypothesis. Results are consistent with prior research that showed no support for the traditional threshold hypothesis and instead found a strong relationship between intelligence and creative achievement beyond the intelligence threshold (Park et al., 2007; Robertson et al., 2010).

Finally, our results suggest that the type of openness needed for intelligence to express itself in the form of creative achievement is domain specific, with achievement in the arts requiring high aesthetic openness and achievement in the sciences requiring high intellect. These results are consistent with prior research that has identified the importance of the aesthetic openness aspect for

creative achievement in the arts and the intellect aspect for creative achievement in the sciences. Like creative achievement broadly, creative achievement in both the arts and sciences exhibited a stronger relationship with intelligence among those that were high in their corresponding openness aspects. In contrast, no significant interactive effects between quadratic intelligence terms and intellect were found for the arts, or between quadratic intelligence terms and aesthetic openness for the sciences.

Our findings are further bolstered by the consistency of variable relationships with those found in other studies as well as the rigor of the methodological approach. Carson et al. (2005) reported a marginally significant correlation between total CAQ scores and intelligence of r = .14, p = .06. Our results show a correlation of identical magnitude but significant at p < .001, likely because of the current study's larger sample size. Results are also consistent with Kaufman et al.'s (2016) investigation of openness aspects and domain specific achievements. Kaufman et al. found correlations between intelligence and CAQ Sciences scores ranging from .11 to .30, and correlations between intelligence and CAQ Arts ranged from -.04 to .18. Our results fall approximately in the middle of these ranges, and CAQ Sciences scores exhibited a stronger correlation with intelligence than did CAQ Arts scores. Further, like Kaufman et al., our results support the importance of aesthetic openness for CAQ Arts scores and intellect for CAQ Sciences scores. Additionally, relationships between openness aspects also correlated with intelligence as expected; fluid intelligence showed a stronger correlation with intellect than with aesthetic openness

(DeYoung, 2011). Although these correlation magnitudes were somewhat lower than those reported by DeYoung (2011), such weaker correlations are typical of nonverbal intelligence measures (e.g., the Sandia Matrices used in this study) relative to verbal measures. Finally, the current study utilized IRT scoring and examined both a full and restricted sample in Poisson regression analyses to ensure that neither measurement error nor the distribution of creative achievements resulted in spurious findings.

The current study included several limitations. First, the current study builds on prior research highlighting the importance of openness for high levels of creative achievement. However, a variety of individual characteristics are known to impact creative potential and creative achievement, including both cognitively and socially oriented personality traits, some clinical personality disorders, and motivation (Feist, 2010). Such characteristics may likewise qualify the relationship between intelligence and creative achivement. For example, in addition to exhibiting high levels of openness, Feist (1998) found that more creative persons are typically less conscientiousness, more self-accepting, and more hostile and impulsive. Additionally, prior research supports the importance of expertise and knowledge mastery for creative thinking and, ultimately, achievement in a given field (e.g., Ericsson, Nandagopal, & Roring, 2005; Ericsson, Roring, & Nandagopal, 2007; Mackinnon, 1962; Vincent, Decker, & Mumford, 2002). Considerations of expertise also open the door to intriguing questions about how expertise may mediate the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement and whether innate abilities such as intelligence are truly necessary for achievement if an individual is afforded sufficient practice or training opportunities (Ericsson et al., 2005). Finally, creative abilities—such as divergent thinking have been shown to be one of the most important predictors of creative achievement (Kim, 2008). Thus, the relationship between intelligence, creative potential or abilities, and creative achievement also warrants further investigation. We encourage researchers to explore the vast array of individual differences that may qualify the intelligence– creativity relationship.

In addition to individual characteristics that likely impact the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement, situational and circumstantial factors may also impact this relationship. Eysenck (1995) proposes that the creative achievement depends on not only intelligence and personality but also environmental factors, including cultural, political and religious, and educational factors. As one reviewer noted, prior research suggests there is no relationship between average national intelligence and creative achievement (Lynn & Meisenberg, 2010; Lynn & Vanhanen, 2012), and the intelligence– creativity relationship seems particularly weak among some Asian populations, which show relatively high intelligence (Lynn & Meisenberg, 2010; Rushton & Jensen, 2005) but low creativity (Kim, Lee, Chae, Anderson, & Laurence, 2011; Niu & Sternberg, 2002, 2003; Nouri et al., 2015; Saeki, Fan, & Van Dusen, 2001). These results are consistent with Eysenck's suggestion that cultural factors may critically moderate the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement. Indeed, researchers have suggested that the negligible intelligence– creativity relationships found among Asian populations may be influenced by the cultural importance of Confucian principles, which can suppress creative behavior (Kim, 2007; Kim et al., 2011), or that Asians conceptualize creativity somewhat differently than do Westerners (Niu & Sternberg, 2002). Similarly,

although the average IQ in the United States has increased over time (Pietschnig & Voracek, 2015), creativity has declined, which Kim (2011) suggests may stem from the emphasis that the United States increasingly places on standardized testing and structured activities for children. Even within a country or national culture, schools' efforts to cultivate climates for creative expression can have a large impact on students' creative achievement (Kim & Kipper, 2016). Thus, the cultural context and sample characteristics of the current study may limit generalizability of the present findings. Future studies should explore the influence of such environmental factors. Investigating a three-way conditional threshold hypothesis between intelligence, personality (e.g., openness), and environmental factors may prove fruitful for clarifying the antecedents of creative achievement.

Finally, the CAQ operationalizes creativity exclusively as formally recognized creative achievements. The present study was concerned with how the threshold hypothesis applies to creative achievement specifically, so the CAQ was appropriate for the current purposes. However, as mentioned previously, at least one study has found support for a curvilinear relationship between intelligence and creative potential that strengthens among those high in intelligence (Sligh et al., 2005). Thus, future studies might consider expanding a version of the conditional threshold hypothesis to divergent thinking or other measures of creative potential. Moreover, as noted by Kaufman et al. (2016), the CAQ is primarily limited to two domains and therefore does not include other avenues for creative achievement, such as business, mechanical, humanities, or social sciences. The application of the threshold hypothesis to other domains of creative achievement should be considered.

The current study revisits the application of the popular threshold hypothesis to creative achievement. We have shown both theoretical and empirical support for a conditional threshold hypothesis rather than the threshold hypothesis as traditionally outlined. This conditional threshold hypothesis suggests not only that the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement is dependent on other characteristics but also that it strengthens as intelligence increases among those with sufficient standing on those characteristics, such as openness to experience. Results provide a path forward for expanding our understanding of the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement, and we encourage further explorations of the conditional-threshold hypothesis, incorporating both openness and other candidates for critical qualifying characteristics.

Supplementary Analyses Using Alternative Creative Achievement Scoring

As described in text, the current study does not utilize the original scoring approach as described by Carson et al. (2005). Instead, we score Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ) data according to a modified approach recently recommended in a personal communication with S. H. Carson (cf. Kaufman et al., 2016). Carson et al.'s original scoring approach recommended multiplying certain advanced achievement levels by the frequency of the accomplishment (e.g., obtaining a grant is a sixth-level achievement; therefore, someone receiving three grants will receive a score of 18 for these achievements) in addition to awarding points per level for all other achievements (e.g., 2 points for indicating achievement at the second level, regardless of frequency). The modified scoring approach does not multiply frequencies and, instead, only awards points per level for achievements.

Understandably, one reviewer was concerned by the use of the modified scoring approach rather than the original scoring. In this Appendix, we provide all descriptive statistics and results as they would appear in text had we used Carson et al.'s (2005) original scoring approach. Table A1 presents descriptive statistics for the CAQ Total, Arts, and Sciences scales. Relative to the modified scoring approach used in text, skew and kurtosis increase dramatically using the original scoring, particularly for the sciences. Under the modified approach utilized by Kaufman et al. (2016), the skew and kurtosis were 1.95 and 4.24 for the CAQ Total score, 2.12 and 4.83 for the CAQ Arts score, and 3.47 and 13.68, for the CAQ Sciences score, respectively. On the other hand, Table A1 shows that using the original scoring approximately doubles the skew and increases kurtosis by a factor of between 6 and 8 for the three CAQ scores. Thus, we utilize the modified scoring suggested by S. H. Carson to Kauffman et al. in the main text.

Table A2 displays the results of Poisson regression analyses for CAQ scores using the original scoring approach regressed on intelligence and trait-level openness. Like those results reported in text, trait-level openness shows a significant interaction with the

quadratic intelligence term for total creative achievement (b=.02, p=.017) and creative achievement in the sciences (b=.20, p<.001). In contrast to results reported in text, there is now no evidence of a significant interaction between trait-level openness and the quadratic intelligence term for creative achievement in the arts (b=.01, p=.210). Nonetheless, the linear interaction term was significant (b=.14, p<.001), and as shown in Figure A1, the forms of the relationships for CAQ scores predicted by intelligence and trait-level openness look very similar to those illustrated by Figure 2 in text.

Table A3 displays the results of Poisson regression analyses for arts and sciences CAQ scores using the original scoring approach regressed on intelligence, aesthetic openness, and intellect. Like those results reported in text, in both the full and reduced samples, aesthetic openness shows a significant interaction with the quadratic intelligence term for creative achievement in the arts (full, b = .03, p < .001; reduced, b = .03, p < .001) and intellect shows a significant interaction with the quadratic intelligence term for creative achievement in the sciences (full, b = .14, p < .001; reduced, b = .09, p < .001). In contrast to results reported in text, there is now also evidence of a significant interaction between intellect and the quadratic intelligence term for creative achievement in the arts in both the full (b = -0.02, p = .004) and reduced (b = -.04, p < .001) samples. Notably, this effect is in the opposite direction of that for the aesthetic openness/quadraticintelligence interaction. However, the form of the relationship is still highly similar to that found in the results reported in the main text. Thus, these results still point to the importance of aesthetic openness relative to intellect for creative achievement in the arts. Further, as shown in Figures A2 and A3, the forms of the relationships for CAQ scores predicted by intelligence and openness aspects look very similar to those illustrated by Figure 3 in the text.

Overall, results using the original CAQ scoring approach closely mirror those using the modified approach presented in text. Although results for creative achievement in the arts predicted by trait-level openness differ slightly, results for creative achievement predicted by the aspects are relatively consistent. Further, we contend that the apparent lack of consistency of the significance of various terms within these sup-

plemental analyses supports the idea that utilizing the original scoring might increase the "noise" in Poisson regression analyses. Given the overall consistency of results but the substantially increased skew using Carson et al.'s (2005) original CAQ scoring approach, we believe the modified scoring as presented in text is most appropriate for the current data but have included these analyses for consideration.
